notes.text: The forward lines keep changing. Even their four most-used trios over the last 10 games cover only 28% of their forwards’ 5-on-5 time, the third-lowest in the league (a typical team: 43%). The lines listed lean on their latest games, but expect new combinations tonight.
Filip Chytil is on injured reserve (upper body injury) and missed their last game. He is one of their most valuable skaters.
Jacob Quillan was added to the roster on Oct 31 and has played beside Linus Karlsson and Liam Öhgren.
Max Sasson has started killing penalties: on the ice for 30% of the team’s shorthanded time in 16 games, up from 4% last season.
Zach Hyman is on injured reserve (neck injury) and has missed the last 2 games. He is a top-six forward. Colton Dach has taken his spot beside Ryan Nugent-Hopkins and Kasperi Kapanen.

Matt Savoie is on long-term injured reserve (lower-body injury) and has not played this season. Leon Draisaitl has taken his spot beside Connor McDavid and Vasily Podkolzin. That line has had 63% of the chances at 5-on-5 in 173:18 together.
Kasperi Kapanen has started playing on the power play: on the ice for 48% of the team’s power-play time in 14 games, up from 6% last season.
Ty Emberson is no longer killing penalties: 5% of the team’s shorthanded time in 12 games, down from 30% last season.

EDM.head: The Oilers should be in control
EDM.body: Even though Edmonton will be without Hyman, the Oilers have been out-chancing opponents by a wide margin lately and have home-ice advantage. If the Canucks want to spoil it, start with getting good looks.

VAN.head: A steep climb for the Canucks
VAN.body: Even though Edmonton will be without Hyman, the Oilers have been out-chancing opponents by a wide margin lately and have home-ice advantage. To pull this off, the Canucks can start with getting good looks, plus Leevi Meriläinen stealing the show.

story.head: McDavid’s favorite opponent
paras: The teams have split two meetings this season. The Oilers have won two in a row, the last a 4-0 rout of the Islanders. The Canucks (3-12-1) lost 4-2 to Toronto on Oct 31. Going in, the Canucks are last in the NHL and the Oil first in the Pacific (third in the NHL).

The Canucks have played better than their record (.219) says: their chances are worth about .311, and their goaltending has held them back. The Oilers’ record (.786) is running ahead of what their chances are worth (.625), largely thanks to their finishing.

The Canucks pick their shots (lowest) and have had shaky goaltending (32nd). They also have a leaky penalty kill (32nd), so the Oilers’ power play (1st) could do real damage when they’re shorthanded. Vancouver has allowed 4.50 goals a game, the most in the league. On the other side, the Oilers lean on their stars more than any team in the league (lowest), have the league’s most dangerous power play (1st) and get their defensemen shooting (3rd). Edmonton has scored 4.21 goals a game, the most in the league. Both teams play slow, low-event hockey, so expect a tight one.

Elias Pettersson (#40) (4 G / 12 A / 16 P in 16 GP) leads the Canucks in scoring, and Jonathan Lekkerimäki (6 G / 7 A / 13 P in 16 GP) has a team-high six goals. Connor McDavid (8 G / 29 A / 37 P in 14 GP) leads the Oilers and the whole NHL in scoring, with eleven points in his last five games and a point in eight straight games against Vancouver. Leon Draisaitl (12 G / 14 A / 26 P in 14 GP) has a team-high twelve goals, tied for second in the NHL, with ten points in his last five games.
Leevi Meriläinen (2-5-1 / .897 SV% in 9 GS) will likely start for Vancouver, and Tristan Jarry (4-1-2 / .895 SV% in 7 GS) for Edmonton.
At home, Mike Babcock likes to send Frederic, Michaels and Howard out against opponents’ fourth lines, so watch for them against Cotter, Sasson and Gallagher.
